In contrast, for discrete oracles with $n_{\text{b}} |{\sin(φ_{0}/{2})}|=Ω(1)$, we provide an algorithm using $O(\max\{1,\sqrt{N/n_{\text{b}}|{\sin(φ_{0}/{2})}|}\})$ queries. We also prove matching lower bounds on the query complexity, showing that these algorithms are asymptotically optimal. Furthermore, we show that, in the absence of loss, non-Gaussianity is necessary to achieve the optimal joint query scaling in $N$ and $n_{\text{b}}$, but entanglement is not. Under uniform boson loss at rate $γ$, we prove a query lower bound of $Ω( γN / n _{\text{b}} B_{0}^{2} )$, attained for $γ= Ω(B_{0} \sqrt{n _{\text{b}}/N})$ using coherent-state probes. Finally, we propose experimental implementations using multipass optical microscopy or superconducting circuits as potential routes to speeding up imaging or device calibration with a low boson-number budget.
2610.17163.why: Optimal bosonic unstructured search scales with mean boson number; non-Gaussianity is necessary but entanglement is not, with matching lower bounds under loss.

2610.14778.title: Avoiding Defects within Heavy-Hexagon Architecture
2610.14778.abstract: When implementing scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing using superconducting quantum processors, one of the critical challenges to overcome is the presence of defective qubits arising from fabrication and calibration imperfections. A defect on a specific qubit severely restricts the connectivity between adjacent qubits, disrupts stabilizer measurements, induces frequent detection events, and consequently inflates the logical error rate. To mitigate this issue, various strategies have been proposed, such as syndrome extraction circuits based on stabilizer folding and the construction of super-stabilizers via gauge operators. However, these methods have primarily been developed for architectures with relatively high connectivity of 3 to 4. Furthermore, experimental demonstrations showing an actual reduction in logical error rates in the presence of physical hardware defects have been lacking. In this work, we propose a defect-avoidance scheme tailored for the heavy-hexagon architecture, which features a lower connectivity of 2 to 3. While previous approaches required four measurement cycles to measure all gauge operators comprising a super-stabilizer, our proposed scheme completes all gauge measurements within only two cycles. We experimentally validate this approach on IBM quantum hardware by identifying physical defects and implementing the defect-avoidance circuits. As a result, avoiding the defect yields an approximately 10\% reduction in the logical error rate per cycle for both logical $X$ and $Z$ errors. These findings demonstrate that defects in superconducting hardware can be successfully handled even under the constrained connectivity of heavy-hexagon lattices, and that defect avoidance substantially reduces logical errors on real quantum hardware.
2610.14778.why: A two-cycle super-stabilizer scheme avoids defective qubits on heavy-hex lattices, cutting logical error per cycle by about 10% on IBM hardware.

2610.19964.title: Preservation of photon statistics upon selective molecular modulation in hollow-core fibers
2610.19964.abstract: Preserving the underlying statistical properties of light during frequency transduction is essential for interfacing spectrally disparate quantum systems. To do this successfully, the process needs to be highly efficient, broadband and noiseless. Despite significant progress in this field, satisfying all these conditions remains challenging. Recently, molecular modulation-based transduction in hollow-core fibers has emerged as a promising approach, where biphoton correlations were proven to be preserved during frequency up-conversion. However, beyond this previous demonstration of correlation-maintaining conversion, whether molecular modulation can preserve more general statistical properties of light remains experimentally unexplored. Here, we demonstrate the conservation of photon-number statistics during selective frequency transduction by Raman molecular modulation in a hydrogen-filled hollow-core fiber. As a proof of concept, weak 585-nm signals are selectively converted to 773 nm in the near-infrared and to 471 nm in the blue spectral region with near-unity efficiencies. Phase matching between the generated coherence waves and the transitions of interest is achieved through the effective dispersion of the system, enabling independent selection of the frequency up- and down-conversion processes. The preservation of the photon-number statistics of the shifted signals, along with the large frequency shifts, broad tunability and compatibility with quantum-optical fields, provides a versatile fiber-based platform for quantum frequency transduction. In particular, the demonstrated interfacing between visible and near-infrared wavelengths using low pump energies and low gas pressures offers a route towards connecting spectrally distinct quantum systems, including quantum emitters, sensors and atomic quantum memories, within hybrid quantum networks.
2610.19964.why: Raman molecular modulation in hydrogen-filled hollow-core fibre converts weak 585 nm light to 773 and 471 nm with near-unity efficiency, preserving photon statistics.

eli5.plain: They shifted the colour of faint light by hundreds of nanometres inside a gas-filled fibre without disturbing its photon counting statistics.
eli5.how: A coherent molecular vibration in hydrogen acts as a frequency shifter; phase matching selects up- or down-conversion.
eli5.matters: Statistics-preserving transduction is the optical analogue of the microwave-to-optical problem the reader's field cares about.
eli5.caveat: Tested with weak classical-like signals, not single photons from an emitter, and noise floors at the single-photon level are not shown.

2610.15749.title: Nonperturbative optomechanics with thin, weakly reflective intracavity dielectrics
2610.15749.abstract: Levitated dielectric sensors are often treated as perturbative probes of a pre-existing optical field. We show that this picture fails for a novel sensor geometry: a dielectric plate whose transverse extent captures the full optical mode. Even an optically thin sensor with modest refractive index can heavily restructure the intracavity fields, effectively partitioning a cavity into two subcavities with substantial cross-coupling and producing new optical resonances and trapping sites with properties which deviate from the standard intuition. Conventional perturbative expressions for the cavity frequency shift and optomechanical coupling depart from the exact solution at thicknesses as small as $\simλ/(10n)$. Furthermore, cavity locking decreases the coupling and increases the trap stiffness by orders of magnitude, and the coupled subcavity structure permits appreciable optical cooling at zero detuning, a distinct behavior unique to this nonperturbative regime. These effects, sharing a common origin, establish a distinct regime of cavity optomechanics in which the sensor is no longer merely a probe of the cavity field, but an element that helps define it.
2610.15749.why: A thin dielectric plate spanning the whole cavity mode splits it into coupled subcavities; perturbative coupling formulas fail already at lambda over 10n thickness.

eli5.plain: Even a very thin glass plate inside a laser cavity reshapes the light so much that the usual approximations break.
eli5.how: Exact field solutions show the plate creates two coupled subcavities with new resonances, changed trap stiffness and cooling at zero detuning.
eli5.matters: A reminder that perturbative coupling formulas fail when the 'probe' defines the mode, a lesson also for large dielectrics in 3D microwave cavities.
eli5.caveat: Classical optics theory aimed at gravitational-wave sensors; no quantum experiment.

2610.19751.title: Quantum-enhanced Search for Galactic Dark Photons Using Cat-State Cavities
2610.19751.abstract: We present a quantum-enhanced search for the Galactic dark-photon background (GDPB), a relativistic and anisotropic vector field that can be produced by dark-matter decay or annihilation in the Milky Way halo. We reinterpret an existing quantum-enhanced dark-photon dataset obtained with a superconducting circuit QED platform originally developed for wave-like dark-photon dark-matter searches, consisting of a high-$Q$ niobium cavity in the $\mathrm{TM}_{010}$ mode dispersively coupled to a transmon qubit. By preparing four-component cat states and performing repeated quantum non-demolition parity measurements, analyzed with a hidden Markov model, we extract photon-transition probabilities for multiple cat amplitudes and integration times. The coupling to the GDPB is governed by a polarization- and angle-dependent cavity overlap function, which predicts a distinctive diurnal modulation of the excitation rate for both longitudinal and transverse polarizations. From the absence of such modulation, we set 90\% confidence-level bounds on the kinetic-mixing parameter $ε$ for two benchmark production mechanisms (parametric and cascade decay) over the relativistic mass range $m_X \ll ω_c$.
2610.19751.why: Re-analysing cat-state parity data from a cavity dark-photon search sets diurnal-modulation bounds on a relativistic Galactic dark-photon background.

eli5.plain: They reused data from a qubit-based dark-matter search to look for a different hypothetical particle stream from our galaxy, and found nothing.
eli5.how: Repeated parity checks on four-component cat states in a niobium cavity count rare photon jumps; a Galactic signal would make that rate rise and fall with Earth's rotation.
eli5.matters: Shows cat-state photon counting with a transmon as a reusable detector platform beyond its original target.
eli5.caveat: No new measurement and a null result; the bounds depend on model-specific production mechanisms and cavity overlap functions.

2610.19904.title: Single and coupled quantum van der Pol oscillators: Wigner-function dynamics, exact qutrit solutions, and synchronization
2610.19904.abstract: We study quantum van der Pol oscillator in which single-photon pumping competes with a nonlinear two-photon dissipative channel to produce a quantum limit cycle, and the question of how two such oscillators with non-identical intrinsic frequencies synchronize in the sense of phase locking when coupled dissipatively to one another. For a single oscillator, starting from a Lindblad description of the dynamics, we derive the exact Wigner-function evolution equation, and show that its Fokker--Planck approximation admits in the appropriate regime an equivalent classical Itô stochastic description that reproduces remarkably well the full Lindblad dynamics. Notably, the stochastic approach provides an efficient means of capturing system dynamics in the semiclassical regime, where a large number of energy eigenstates contribute and direct numerical simulations become computationally demanding. Restricting to the three lowest Fock states and using a parity symmetry, we obtain in closed form the stationary-state density matrix and its Wigner-function representation that displays pronounced nonclassical features. For two non-identical oscillators, we study the full Lindblad dynamics numerically and characterize synchronization through the stationary-state order parameter as a function of frequency mismatch and dissipative coupling. We find that increasing the effective nonlinear dissipative strength suppresses the synchronized region. Restricting the two oscillators to the three-level qutrit subspace, a parity symmetry reduces the stationary-state problem to an exact $41$-dimensional linear system, allowing to compute the synchronization order parameter. In this reduced description, results in the limit of large dissipation agree closely with those from the full dynamics, while exhibiting in the limit of small dissipation a double-peak synchronization structure accompanied by a phase reversal.
2610.19904.why: Exact qutrit solutions and a stochastic Wigner method describe quantum van der Pol limit cycles; strong nonlinear dissipation shrinks the synchronisation region.

eli5.plain: A theory study of the simplest quantum self-oscillator and how two of them lock together.
eli5.how: Restricting to three Fock levels with a parity symmetry gives closed-form steady states; a Fokker-Planck reduction captures the semiclassical regime.
eli5.matters: Two-photon loss and single-photon gain are realisable with parametrically pumped superconducting resonators.
eli5.caveat: Analytic results hold in the deep-quantum qutrit truncation; experimental signatures are not proposed.

2610.17855.title: Emergent Non-Biorthogonal Born Rule at Dynamical Quantum Phase Transitions
2610.17855.abstract: Non-Hermitian dynamics possesses distinct left and right eigenstates, but their normalization freedom obscures a direct probabilistic interpretation. Starting from a globally Hermitian system governed by the standard Born rule, we generalize dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) from a reference state to a physical subspace. This generalization provides a clear probabilistic interpretation of left and right states: when each state is normalized to itself, their mutual overlap determines a directly accessible dynamical transition rate. We discuss the new phenomena governed by this emergent non-biorthogonal Born rule and further identify a class of exceptional-point DQPTs (EP-DQPTs), at which the eigenstates of the critical propagator coalesce. Our theory places the probabilistic interpretation of non-Hermitian quantum mechanics on the firm footing of Hermitian quantum mechanics.
2610.17855.why: Generalising dynamical quantum phase transitions to subspaces gives left and right non-Hermitian eigenstates a direct Born-rule probabilistic meaning.

eli5.plain: They give a clear physical probability meaning to the two different kinds of states that appear in non-Hermitian quantum mechanics.
eli5.how: Starting from ordinary Hermitian dynamics, transition rates between subspaces involve the overlap of self-normalised left and right states.
eli5.matters: Non-Hermitian effective models are common for lossy microwave systems; this grounds how to read their probabilities.
eli5.caveat: A reinterpretation within standard quantum mechanics, not a modification of the Born rule.

2610.21399.title: Nonreciprocal Control of Spatiotemporal Floquet Dynamics in Levitated Optomechanical Arrays
2610.21399.abstract: Periodically driven photonic and optomechanical systems provide a versatile setting for realizing collective Floquet dynamics, yet the relation between temporal locking and continuous rotation of the finite-$q$ pattern remains poorly understood. We show that a nonreciprocal ring of parametrically driven optically levitated particles allows the spatial phase to be controlled while collective temporal locking is preserved. Nonreciprocity polarizes the counterpropagating finite-wave-vector modes and drives a transition from the pinned state to persistent directional spatial-phase drift. The normalized spatial-phase drift velocity is independently encoded in the splitting of the two dominant spectral branches, and its direction reverses with the coupling asymmetry. The pinned regime exhibits a laboratory frame period-two time-crystalline response, whereas the rotating regime forms a distinct temporally locked spatiotemporally ordered state. The same correspondence between spatial-phase drift and spectral splitting persists down to few-particle rings, indicating that the effect does not require a large array. These results establish nonreciprocity as a route to independently control spatial-phase drift and temporal synchronization in driven levitated optomechanical systems.
2610.21399.why: Nonreciprocal coupling in a ring of levitated particles drives a transition from pinned period-two locking to a rotating spatiotemporally ordered state.

2610.20314.title: Coherent and dissipative coupling of multiple photon-magnon hybrids in a chiral microwave resonator
2610.20314.abstract: We demonstrate control between level repulsion and level attraction of photon-magnon coupling spectra in a chiral microwave-photon resonator loaded with a 2 mm YIG sphere. By systematically varying the coupling mode volume via the YIG position and the dc-field orientation, we tune the ratio between coherent and dissipative coupling strengths, $J/Γ$, and thereby switch between level repulsion and level attraction in the hybrid spectra. Full-wave electromagnetic and magnetization-dynamics simulations reveal multiple photon-magnon hybrid modes with distinct spatial overlap factors, which quantitatively account for gap sizes and their angular dependence. Strong nonreciprocity appears near $J/Γ\approx 1$, yielding 28.6 dB isolation ratio in agreement with a unified single-bath input-output model and full-wave simulations. Angular dependence of spectral characterization confirms a picture of the chirality-selection rule and our method of geometric tuning might be useful for considering reconfigurable on-chip isolators.
2610.20314.why: Tuning YIG position and field angle in a chiral resonator switches photon-magnon coupling between repulsion and attraction, giving 28.6 dB nonreciprocal isolation.

eli5.plain: They moved a magnetic sphere inside a microwave circuit to switch how it hybridises with the photons, and got a one-way device out of it.
eli5.how: Coherent and dissipative coupling compete; their ratio, set by geometry and field orientation, decides whether modes repel or attract, and near balance transmission becomes direction-dependent.
eli5.matters: A geometric route to tunable on-chip isolators is of practical interest for microwave readout chains.
eli5.caveat: Room-temperature-style classical spectroscopy on a millimetre YIG sphere; compatibility with millikelvin superconducting circuits is not shown.

2610.18482.title: Lifting: Quantum State Discrimination Framework for Mid-Circuit Measurements
2610.18482.abstract: Quantum computing promises new capabilities beyond classical computation. Mid-circuit measurements (MCMs) enable error correction and outcome-dependent control, but their reliability is limited by noise on superconducting hardware. These operations depend on accurate quantum state discrimination (QSD), which assigns measured signals to state labels. Neural network-based (NN-based) QSD improves this assignment, yet its error remains bounded below by the Bayes risk of the available readout distributions. A complementary challenge is state deterioration as successive measurements accumulate and circuit execution advances, making static calibration less representative of the workload. We present Lifting, a QSD framework that addresses both challenges through repetition encoding, neural decoding, and in situ calibration. Encoding supplies joint in-phase and quadrature (I-Q) readout signals from the target and auxiliary qubits, while contextual calibration trains the decoder for the conditions encountered during execution. Our theoretical analysis shows that retaining additional channels from a fixed joint distribution cannot increase Bayes risk and establishes sufficient conditions for contraction of an overlap-based upper bound. Experiments across three IBM processors evaluate the framework on repeated stabilizer measurement, parity-check, and teleportation workloads.
2610.18482.why: Repetition encoding plus in-situ-calibrated neural decoding improves mid-circuit state discrimination on three IBM processors.

2610.17367.title: Periodic-Pulse Control of Collective Emission and Photon Statistics in Interacting Quantum Emitters
2610.17367.abstract: We investigate the collective emission spectra and photon correlations of two identical dipole-dipole-coupled emitters under continuous-wave (CW) and periodic pulsed driving. Our results show that a periodic train of instantaneous $π_x$ pulses can generate emission spectra whose dominant features closely resemble those obtained under CW excitation. We find that the structure of the collective emission spectra reflects the interplay among the resonance conditions, dipole-dipole coupling, and the inter-pulse delay $τ_D$. We further demonstrate that finite-duration $π_x$ pulses with sufficiently high Rabi frequencies can closely reproduce the ideal instantaneous-pulse limit. In contrast to the emission spectra, the photon correlations $g^{(2)}(t,τ)$ are governed primarily by $τ_D$ and, unlike under CW driving, become increasingly insensitive to the resonance conditions in the short-pulse limit. These results establish periodic pulsed driving as a versatile means of tailoring both the emission spectra and the photon statistics of coupled two-emitter systems.
2610.17367.why: Periodic pi-pulse trains reproduce CW collective emission spectra of two dipole-coupled emitters while making g2 depend mainly on the inter-pulse delay.

2610.19599.title: Cryogenic Multiplexing Control Chip for Superconducting Quantum Processor
2610.19599.abstract: This paper proposes a scheme and design of cryogenic multiplexing control chip (MCC) which enables one microwave cable to control many superconducting qubits. Designed based on adjustable inductor, MCC is a non-reciprocal device which generates microwave signals between 4 and 8 GHz and constructs XY control circuit to operate qubits. The effects of filters, isolators, power splitters, qubits and load impedance on MCC are analyzed in the frequency-domain simulation. And in time-domain simulation, the response time, Gaussian pulses, single-sideband, amplitude and frequency compensation of MCC are examined. The MCC can be integrated with the superconducting qubits on the same package at 20 mK temperature stage, and output specific microwave pulses used to drive the superconducting qubits without crosstalks. The MCC can greatly reduce the number of microwave control lines and is beneficial to the development of large-scale superconducting quantum processor.
2610.19599.why: Simulated cryogenic adjustable-inductor chip would generate 4-8 GHz XY pulses for many qubits over one cable; no measured device.

2610.15200.title: Local Suppression of Superconductivity in Niobium Films by Focused Silicon Ion Implantation
2610.15200.abstract: Magnetic flux trapped in a superconducting circuit shifts the critical currents of nearby Josephson junctions and disturbs the operation of the circuit. The usual remedy is a moat etched through the ground plane to hold the flux away from the logic. We report direct write silicon ion implantation with a focused ion beam as a way to make moats without etching the film, by locally suppressing superconductivity in niobium (Nb). Single implanted lines were written across Nb electrodes in films of three thicknesses over two orders of magnitude in ion fluence, and the transition temperature, resistance, and critical current density of each line were measured. The transition temperature of the line falls with fluence while the surrounding Nb is unchanged, and the critical current density falls by about two orders of magnitude before the line becomes resistive at 4.2 K. The product of the critical current and the resistance of the lines follows a single power law in reduced temperature. This gives an estimate of the critical current of a line at any temperature from its transition temperature and resistance. A time dependent Ginzburg-Landau simulation indicates that an implanted region can capture and hold a vortex. From these results we suggest a starting ion energy and fluence for implanted moats in a 100 nm Nb ground plane at 4.2 K and estimate the equivalent broad beam fluence.
2610.15200.why: Focused silicon ion implantation locally suppresses Nb superconductivity, offering etch-free flux-trapping moats with a calibrated fluence recipe.

2610.22004.title: Thermal activation of photon catalysis in difference-intensity Mach-Zehnder interferometry with squeezed thermal light
2610.22004.abstract: Realistic non-Gaussian operations, which can be implemented by mixing a nonclassical Gaussian state with a Fock state at a beam splitter and then heralding on a photon-number-resolving detector, are known to improve phase estimation in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer. The existing studies have considered the single-mode squeezed vacuum for difference-intensity and parity detection, and the two-mode squeezed thermal state for parity detection alone as the initial Gaussian resources. However, a real squeezer in the lab actually produces single-mode squeezed thermal light, which has not been studied in a coherent-plus-resource interferometer. We take up this case and using the phase space Wigner picture, we obtain the heralded state produced by photon subtraction, addition and catalysis on a single-mode squeezed thermal resource, and evaluate the corresponding phase sensitivities. Single-photon catalysis, which is useless on squeezed vacuum, becomes a useful operation for any thermal occupation above $\nth\simeq0.2$, and since it heralds with a probability near one-half, it turns out to be the best success-weighted operation over the whole thermal range. In the vacuum limit our results reproduce the known hierarchy, where two-photon catalysis is the best operation. The quantum Fisher information computations confirms that thermal noise enhances the phase information encoded in the catalyzed state, demonstrating that difference-intensity detection closely approaches the ultimate precision bound across most operational regimes, and, together with a loss analysis, verifies the robustness of the effect.
2610.22004.why: Single-photon catalysis on squeezed thermal light becomes useful above 0.2 thermal photons and is the best success-weighted operation for phase estimation.

2610.15827.title: Photon-efficient readout of optical cavity arrays via spatial heterodyne
2610.15827.abstract: Optical cavity arrays are an emerging tool for efficiently interfacing optical photons to quantum emitters for applications such as quantum computing. In this work, we demonstrate a metrology technique for such cavity arrays by interfering cavity array outputs against a tilted reference beam on a camera, constituting a spatial heterodyne. Both the amplitude and phase of each cavity's transmitted field can be extracted from the resulting images. Enabled by the improved scaling of heterodyne detection over intensity detection in the presence of technical noise, we demonstrate signal-to-noise ratio greater than one down to the single detected photon level, even in the presence of hundreds of noise equivalent photons. This readout technique holds promise for fast, non-destructive imaging of atomic qubits in cavity arrays by requiring fewer scattered photons while allowing the use of fast cameras with higher electronic readout noise.
2610.15827.why: Spatial heterodyne imaging reads amplitude and phase of every cavity in an optical array at single-detected-photon SNR above one.

2610.17475.title: Mathematical framework for simulation of non-perturbative cavity optomechanics with plate-like dielectrics
2610.17475.abstract: Cavity optomechanical models typically treat a sensor either as a perturbative polarizable object in a pre-existing optical field, or solve the field at a fixed equilibrium and linearize in a fixed optical-mode basis. Neither self-consistently determines the spatially resolved cavity field, the optical force, the mechanical equilibrium, and the back-action when a finite-thickness dielectric plate intercepts the entire optical mode and restructures the intracavity field. In this companion paper to [1], we develop that treatment by extending the vacuum two-photon formalism to finite-thickness planar dielectrics, incorporating their Fresnel reflection, internal propagation, optical forces, and mechanical back-action directly into the field equations. We derive the carrier and sideband transfer functions needed to describe the coupled optical-mechanical system, including optomechanical cooling and the response to external perturbations. The result is a systematic starting point for calculating detector response and noise budgets for cavity experiments with intracavity dielectrics, including gravitational wave detectors deploying levitated sensors.
2610.17475.why: Companion framework extends the two-photon formalism to finite-thickness dielectrics for self-consistent optomechanical transfer functions.

2610.19905.title: On the structure of low-rank PPT entangled states violating Peres conjecture
2610.19905.abstract: Bound-entangled states with positive partial transpose (PPT) can exhibit quantum steering and Bell nonlocality, disproving the long-standing Peres conjecture and its stronger steering counterpart. These counterexamples, obtained through explicit constructions or numerical searches, raise the question of whether they share a common structural origin. We address this question in the low-rank regime by asking whether known counterexamples can be obtained, up to invertible local filtering, from the complement of an unextendible product basis (UPB). We find that the answer depends crucially on the local dimension. In $3\otimes3$, the rank-four structure of PPT entangled states implies that both the steerable PPT state of Moroder \textit{et al.} and the Bell-nonlocal PPT state of Vértesi and Brunner can be obtained from UPB-complement states under invertible local filtering. For three qubits, in contrast, rank-four states that are PPT across every bipartition are separable across each cut. Moreover, comparison of the product-vector structure of the relevant kernels shows that the known three-qubit Bell-nonlocal PPT states cannot be obtained by invertible local filtering from the complement of any three-qubit UPB. Going beyond rank four, we further show that a known rank-eight three-qutrit state, supported on the complement of a UPB and PPT across every bipartition, is genuinely multipartite entangled. These results show that UPBs provide a unifying structural origin for important low-rank PPT entangled states in $3\otimes3$, but that nonlocal bound entanglement is not, in general, a UPB phenomenon.
2610.19905.why: Known steerable and Bell-nonlocal PPT states in 3x3 come from UPB complements by local filtering, but three-qubit Bell-nonlocal PPT states do not.

eli5.plain: They classify where unusual weakly entangled states that still violate Bell inequalities come from.
eli5.how: Comparing kernel product-vector structure under invertible local filtering against unextendible product bases.
eli5.matters: Bears on the structure of nonlocality, though far from experiment.
eli5.caveat: Purely mathematical with low-rank, low-dimensional scope.

2610.20855.title: Perfect and peak state transfer on IBM quantum hardware
2610.20855.abstract: We run continuous-time quantum walks with perfect and peak state transfer on a present-day superconducting quantum processor, IBM Quantum's $156$-qubit Heron device ibm_kingston, deliberately without error correction or error mitigation. Perfect state transfer and its relaxations have been studied extensively in algebraic graph theory, where one can prove exactly which graphs move a quantum state from one vertex to another with probability one (or with the largest probability the graph allows, in the case of peak state transfer), and at what time. Our experiments cover perfect state transfer on the hypercubes $Q_2 = C_4$ and $Q_3$, and on the Hamming-weighted paths $\mathrm{HP}_n$, the equitable-partition quotients of the hypercubes $Q_n$, for $n$ up to $20$; peak state transfer on the $X_n$ family for $n$ up to $11$; and, for comparison, moving the state along a path of qubits by a sequence of SWAP gates.
2610.20855.why: Perfect and peak state transfer graph walks run unmitigated on a 156-qubit Heron device; mainly an algebraic-graph-theory benchmark.

2610.20268.title: Transport regimes in tunnel ferromagnetic Josephson junctions
2610.20268.abstract: We present a systematic study of the temperature-dependent transport properties of Nb- and Al-based superconductor--insulator--thin superconductor--ferromagnet--superconductor (SIsFS) Josephson junctions. By varying the superconducting material and the thickness of the intermediate superconducting layer, we identify three distinct transport regimes: a tunnel-dominated SIS-like regime, a temperature-driven crossover, and a complex weak-link regime. A unified Usadel-based description connects these regimes through the self-consistent pair potential of the intermediate s-layer. While for Al-based devices an SIS-like transport regime is observed, a self-consistent calculation of the s/F/S proximity electrode, combined with perturbative tunnel coupling to the outer electrode, accounts for Nb devices with different thickness of the superconducting interlayer. The calculation places the 10-nm-interlayer sample in a proximity-supported, strongly suppressed s state, close to the SInFS limit in which the interlayer is effectively driven normal (\textit{n}). A reduced nonlinear long-junction description captures the same limiting physics. The evolution of I_cR_N(T) thereby provides a direct experimental signature of the three transport regimes. Beyond the fundamental interest, the results establish practical design guidelines: Nb junctions with sufficiently thick s interlayers are well suited for high-speed cryogenic memory elements and tunable superconducting parametric amplifiers, while Al junctions are natural candidates for coherent superconducting quantum circuits
2610.20268.why: SIsFS Josephson junctions show three transport regimes set by interlayer thickness, captured by a self-consistent Usadel model.

2610.22737.title: Metric and Dispersive Dynamics of Phase Perturbations in Bohmian Quantum Mechanics
2610.22737.abstract: By linearizing the hydrodynamic equations associated with the Madelung transformation in the context of Bohmian dynamics, we derive an effective metric for the phase perturbation around a background state. We show that the metric previously obtained previously by the same authors arises naturally as a particular case of a more general structure, in which the complete functional variation of the quantum potential is retained and external classical potentials can be incorporated. This generalization preserves the dependence of the quantum potential on the density and its spatial derivatives, generating additional terms that introduce dispersive corrections and act as sources in the effective Klein-Gordon equation. To organize these contributions, we introduce differential operators that separate the local sector responsible for the effective geometry from the corrections associated with the complete functional structure of the quantum potential. We identify the conditions under which these additional terms become negligible, recovering homogeneous propagation and the effective geometry for the Gaussian wave packet of a free particle.
2610.22737.why: Linearised Madelung hydrodynamics in Bohmian mechanics gives an effective metric for phase perturbations, with dispersive corrections from the full quantum potential.

eli5.plain: They describe small ripples in the phase of a Bohmian wave as waves in an effective curved space.
eli5.how: Linearising the hydrodynamic form of the Schrödinger equation yields a Klein-Gordon-like equation with extra dispersive terms.
eli5.matters: An analogue-gravity reading of the pilot-wave picture.
eli5.caveat: No new prediction beyond standard quantum mechanics.

2610.16468.title: Deterministic positioning accuracy of B centers in hBN by electron irradiation
2610.16468.abstract: Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is a promising material platform for quantum technologies, enabling both the realization of nanophotonic devices and the hosting of point defects that act as high-quality single-photon emitters (SPEs). Among these defects, B centers, which reproducibly emit at 436 nm, can be generated individually at predefined positions using electron beam irradiation, a crucial capability for top-down quantum photonics. Yet, the spatial accuracy of emitter creation strongly conditions the potential applications. Here, we generate arrays of individual B centers in a scanning electron microscope (SEM) with in-situ cathodoluminescence (CL) monitoring. We characterize the sources of random deviations from the target positions to identify the limitations to their deterministic positioning. In particular, we measure the distance between the electron beam and the emitter at the moment the emitter is created based on CL mapping. This approach provides a direct estimation of the spatial extent of the beam-emitter interaction. We find this contribution to be the main constraint to the emitter fabrication accuracy, yielding a standard deviation of 27 nm. Additional contributions, primarily from the finite density of UV-emitting carbon dimer precursors, increase the overall positional standard deviation to 40 nm. Our results highlight the possible improvements to the B center creation technique to reach sub-10 nm accuracy.
2610.16468.why: Cathodoluminescence-monitored electron irradiation places hBN B centers with 40 nm accuracy, limited mainly by the beam-emitter interaction size.

2610.16483.title: Molecule-intercalated van der Waals Josephson junctions uncover complex multiband superconductivity
2610.16483.abstract: Intercalation of molecular species provides a route to tailor the electronic structure in van der Waals superconductors, yet intercalated compounds have rarely been integrated into phase-sensitive quantum devices. Here, we realize hybrid molecular Josephson junctions based on TaS2/NbSe2 heterostructures. Selective intercalation of the TaS2 electrode induces monolayer-like Ising superconductivity, while the junctions exhibit asymmetric Fraunhofer interference, field-induced and spontaneous Josephson diode effects. The zero-field diode disappears upon reversing the electrode stacking and re-emerges after intercalating the lower NbSe2 electrode. These findings indicate that the hybrid superconducting electrode hosts unconventional superconductivity underlying the nonreciprocal transport, while molecular intercalation acts as a tuning knob for its internal phase structure. This behavior is consistent with a time-reversal-symmetry-breaking multiband superconducting state characterized by a nontrivial relative phase between superconducting condensates. Our results establish hybrid molecular Josephson junctions as a quantum-device platform for phase-sensitive investigation and integration of molecularly engineered superconductors, opening opportunities to uncover and engineer unconventional superconducting phases.
2610.16483.why: Molecular intercalation of TaS2/NbSe2 junctions switches a zero-field Josephson diode on and off, hinting at time-reversal-breaking multiband pairing.

2610.23106.title: From quantum emitters to technological platforms: a perspective on semiconductor quantum dots
2610.23106.abstract: Photonic quantum technologies are based on controlled photon states. To generate these, quantum dots have emerged as excellent sources of single and entangled photons. In this Perspective, we briefly review the chronological development of quantum dots as photon sources, from their beginnings as quantum emitters in the early 2000s to the advanced photonic devices being developed today. We highlight the interplay between fundamental research and industrial aspects before discussing the photonic quantum technologies we expect to emerge in the near future.
2610.23106.why: Perspective tracing quantum dots from single emitters to industrial photonic devices; no new results.

2610.22574.title: Two-photon Doppler-free spectroscopy of the $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6s23s\;^1S_0$ Rydberg transition for quantum sensing in ytterbium
2610.22574.abstract: Here we report atomic structure calculations and experimental observations of the two-photon $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6s23s\;^1S_0$ transition in Yb. The unique level structure of Yb places the $6s6p\;^1P_1$ state's energy at $\approx\!49.7\%$ of the ionization energy, which facilitates two-photon Doppler-free excitation of the $6s23s\;^1S_0$ Rydberg state from the $6s^2\;^1S_0$ ground state at a relatively low optical intensity. This $J= 0 \rightarrow J=0$ transition is immune to first-order Zeeman and electric quadrupole shifts, has reduced sensitivity to higher-order Zeeman shifts, and is further predicted to have relatively low sensitivity to density shifts. Using configuration interaction theory, we compute relevant properties of the $6s23s\;^1S_0$ Rydberg state for sensing, including the $C_6$ coefficient, dc polarizability, blackbody radiation (BBR) shift, and BBR depopulation rate. As a first experimental step, we demonstrate two-photon Doppler-free spectroscopy of the $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6s23s\;^1S_0$ transition. From our experimental spectra, we estimate the natural linewidth (lifetime) of the $6s23s\;^1S_0$ state to be 90 kHz (1.8 $μ$s). We believe this transition, or other $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6sns\;^1S_0$ transitions in Yb with $n\approx23$, may find use in a variety of sensing applications, potentially including a two-photon clock, electrometer, or BBR thermometer.
2610.22574.why: Doppler-free two-photon spectroscopy of a Yb J=0 Rydberg transition measures a 90 kHz linewidth for clock and electrometry use.

2610.16806.title: Cavity-modified static polarizabilities of atoms and small molecules within QED full configuration interaction
2610.16806.abstract: Static dipole polarizabilities of H$_2$, LiH, and helium confined in a single-mode optical cavity are computed using quantum-electrodynamical full configuration interaction (QED-FCI). Response properties are obtained as finite-field derivatives of the coupled electron-photon energy. The cavity-induced modification is found to arise from the competition of two contributions of opposite sign, the dipole self-energy and photon exchange, whose relative strength depends on both the cavity frequency and the number of photons involved in the exchange. The residual change suppresses the response of the molecular ground electronic states. For the metastable states of helium atom this balance changes qualitatively, and the differential response of the $2\,^3S_1 \to 2\,^1S_0$ clock transition, which governs its sensitivity to static electric fields and to thermal radiation, is strongly enhanced instead. Cavity confinement can therefore either reduce or increase the dc Stark and blackbody-radiation shifts of a frequency standard, depending on the electronic structure of the states involved. The reported data serve as a reference for cavity-modified response and underscore the need for an exact treatment of light-matter correlation in cavity-QED predictions.
2610.16806.why: QED full configuration interaction shows cavities can suppress or enhance static polarisabilities, including the helium 2S clock transition.

2610.15783.title: Violation of Bell-type Inequality in the Hanbury Brown-Twiss (HBT) Toy-Model: Quantum Correlations beyond Local-Realism
2610.15783.abstract: The Hanbury Brown-Twiss (HBT) effect marked a significant milestone in quantum optics by illustrating that intensity correlations can reveal inherently quantum features of light. Motivated by the structure of the original 8-mode HBT interferometer, we develop a simplified 4-mode toy-model that captures its essential physical ingredients while significantly reducing analytical complexity. Our toy-model provides an intuitive and well-structured framework for examining the desired correlation functions. We investigate whether our toy-model can exhibit genuinely non-classical behaviour by formulating and applying a Bell-type inequality tailored to its specific measurement configuration. Our analysis shows that the correlations generated by the toy-model violate the inequality, indicating the presence of non-local features that are incompatible with any classical hidden-variable description. The results highlight the power of simplified models in uncovering fundamental aspects of non-classicality in optical systems.
2610.15783.why: A four-mode Hanbury Brown-Twiss toy model violates a tailored Bell-type inequality.

eli5.plain: A simplified intensity-interferometer model that they show breaks a classical correlation limit.
eli5.how: A reduced four-mode model replaces the full eight-mode interferometer and a custom inequality is tested.
eli5.matters: Intensity correlations are the bread and butter of microwave photon statistics.
eli5.caveat: A tailored inequality in a toy model; loopholes and experiment are not addressed.

2610.17773.title: Boson Sampling Using Fock States from On-Demand Single Photon Source Arrays: Quantum Complexity & Impact of Dephasing
2610.17773.abstract: Boson sampling with array of on-demand single photons (discreet variable Fock states) as resource states provides distinct advantages in complexity scaling compared to single photon resource states mimicked by the states (continuous variable) generated in nonlinear photonics. Recent progress in realization of regular ordered array of mesa top single quantum dots (MTSQDs) enabling on-demand generation of many photon resource states with high single photon purity and indistinguishability [1,2] has opened the possibility of implementing chip-scale Boson sampling with single photons. An important question towards scale up of such circuits is how the dephasing and decay timescale of individual on-demand single photons affect the final probability distribution of the N-photon entangled state. In this work we report a framework that provides direct link between the physical sources of decoherence to the outcome of multiphoton correlation measurements. We explicitly incorporate the symmetrization of the N-photon states while accounting for the shape of the individual wave packets and dephasing. Using this framework, we show predictive estimates of the probability of generation of a 4-photon NOON state using an optical circuit initialized with 4 identical single photon wave packets, mimicking the emitted photons from MTSQD single photon sources reported in [2]. Specifically, we show how the probability of generating various 4-photon entangled states depend on the two-photon interference visibility which is determined by the pure dephasing timescale in relation to the radiative decay timescale. The results provide quantitative guidelines to measure 4 photon and higher number of entangled photon states generated in an optical circuit with on demand single photon sources and provide a link between physical processes such as temperature and the output state of the quantum optical circuits.
2610.17773.why: Model links quantum-dot dephasing to four-photon NOON-state probabilities in boson-sampling circuits.

2610.17257.title: Turning a superconducting diode into a Feynman ratchet to realize a nanoscale heat engine
2610.17257.abstract: Feynman's ratchet illustrates how work can be extracted from thermal fluctuations in the presence of two heat baths at different temperatures. While some experimental realizations of the ratchet effect have been studied, most lack miniaturization, which is important for some applications. Here, we propose a physical implementation of Feynman's ratchet based on Josephson junctions exhibiting the superconducting diode effect. This setup functions as a heat engine that generates work solely from a temperature gradient via thermal fluctuations. We analyze its output power and efficiency, and, through the Seebeck coefficient, identify the conditions under which the device operates in reverse, functioning instead as a Peltier cooler.
2610.17257.why: A superconducting-diode Josephson junction is proposed as a Feynman ratchet heat engine, with conditions for Peltier-cooler operation.

2610.20148.title: Loss-Tolerant Measurement-Device-Independent QKD over Untrusted Repeaters via High-Dimensional Time-Bin Multiplexing
2610.20148.abstract: We propose a loss-tolerant measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) protocol using time-bin-multiplexed single photons entangled with local qubits stored in nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers. In each round, Alice and Bob each send a single multiplexed photon to an untrusted intermediary, Charlie. Each photon first becomes entangled with Charlie's NV-center qubits; Charlie then performs entanglement swapping between his NV qubits to establish EPR pairs between Alice's and Bob's local qubits. With $d$ time bins per photon, $\log_2 d + 1$ EPR pairs can be generated per transmitted photon, substantially increasing the probability of EPR-pair creation under limited channel bandwidth. To further mitigate the effects of prolonged memory storage, the protocol employs a memory-insensitive (MI) architecture, where multiple banks of qubits and multiplexed photon routing reduce the effective memory lifetime requirements. This approach enhances loss tolerance, enabling higher secret key rates and secure key distribution over longer distances compared to conventional single-photon protocols. Using the Lo-Chau EPR-QKD framework and Shor-Preskill reduction, we prove that the protocol is secure without trusting intermediate nodes, making it suitable for quantum networks with untrusted repeaters.
2610.20148.why: MDI-QKD with time-bin-multiplexed photons and NV-center memories at an untrusted node raises EPR-pair yield per photon.

2610.20040.title: Advances in quantum optomechanical control based on cavity cold-atom systems
2610.20040.abstract: Cavity optomechanics represents a frontier research direction in quantum science and technology, centered on the control and exploration of interactions between electromagnetic fields and mechanical motion. Rooted in quantum mechanics, this field realizes efficient coupling and precise manipulation of optical fields and mechanical vibrations through the structural design and precise regulation of optical microcavities and mechanical oscillators, thereby revealing and harnessing novel quantum phenomena. In recent years, cavity optomechanics has evolved into an interdisciplinary frontier integrating quantum optics, condensed matter physics, and quantum precision measurement, exhibiting profound application in both fundamental physics research and quantum information science. With advancements in technologies such as nanomanufacturing and laser cooling, optomechanical interactions have been successfully demonstrated in various experimental systems. Among these platforms, cavity cold-atom systems stand out as one of the ideal platforms for implementing quantum optomechanics. Featuring exceptional environmental isolation, long quantum coherence times, and strong light-matter interaction, these systems provide a crucial testbed for exploring strong and even ultrastrong optomechanical coupling effects as well as rich nonlinear quantum phenomena. This paper reviews the recent progress in optomechanical control and manipulation based on cavity cold-atom systems. We first outline the fundamental principles of standard cavity optomechanical systems. Then, we describe the experimental realization of linear and nonlinear optomechanical couplings in cold-atom systems. After that, we focus on the representative applications of this platform in high-precision quantum sensing, quantum memory, and the preparation of macroscopic nonclassical states. Finally, we give an outlook and challenges in this field.
2610.20040.why: Review of optomechanical control in cavity cold-atom systems.

2610.18049.title: Scalable long-distance quantum fan-out gates with reduced resource overhead
2610.18049.abstract: Scalable long-distance quantum gates are essential for distributed quantum computation and scalable quantum networks. We propose an efficient scheme for implementing an $n$-qubit fan-out gate $C^n$ (also known as a controlled-NOT-$\cdots$-NOT gate) across spatially separated parties. Our protocol requires only a pre-shared $n$-qubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state, $n$ local controlled-NOT (CNOT) gates, and feed-forward operations, thereby reducing both the CNOT and Hadamard gate counts by $(n-2)$ when compared with the standard decomposition-based approach. We further develop two optical architectures to implement the heralded and post-selected $n$-photon fan-out gates, respectively. These schemes require fewer single photons resources and achieve higher success probabilities than their decomposition-based counterparts, representing significant improvements. The results indicate that our approach is experimentally feasible and pave the way toward practical long-distance quantum computation.
2610.18049.why: GHZ-assisted n-qubit fan-out gate saves n-2 CNOTs, with heralded and post-selected linear-optics versions.

2610.19569.title: A Reconstruction of Michelson Interference from On--Off Detection Statistics
2610.19569.abstract: This paper reconstructs the Michelson interference phenomenon based solely on the binary (on-off) statistics of a single-photon counter and macroscopic path-difference data, without the a priori assumptions of complex wave superposition or prior spectral information. In contrast to the conventional approach that assumes light as a continuous complex wave function and considers interference between them, this study focuses on the algebraic properties inherent in discrete detection statistics. We verify that the discrete response data collected across various path differences form a positive semi-definite matrix, and apply Herglotz's theorem to this result. Consequently, we show that the harmonic form of the interference fringe is not a consequence of adopting a wave model as an axiom, but rather it is uniquely decomposed into a cosine average of wavenumbers dictated by testable algebraic constraints satisfied by the statistical data. Through this approach, the logical basis of the interference phenomenon can be described by the characteristics of the binary data itself, perfectly aligning with the modern optical experimental environment that relies entirely on discrete event statistics.
2610.19569.why: Michelson fringes reconstructed from on-off click statistics via Herglotz's theorem, without assuming wave superposition.

2610.21765.title: Local finite rate semi device independent randomness expansion from quantum contextuality
2610.21765.abstract: Finite rate randomness expansion (RE) which is secure against quantum adversaries is a crucial information processing task which is well studied in the case of two non-communicating parties sharing Bell non-local correlations in a device independent manner. In this paper we show that contextual correlations with only a single localized party are sufficient for RE in a semi-device independent (SDI) manner. We propose a template SDI-RE protocol which is applicable for arbitrary $N$-cycle non-contextuality (NC) inequalities and derive its RE rate under finite statistics. As a special case, we also highlight the advantages of the situation when RE is constrained by Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) inequality but with characterized measurements implemented by only a single party. Our template protocol also incorporates non-ideal statistics which may not satisfy perfect commutativity and perfect repeatability, both of which are necessary in a loophole-free test of NC inequalities. As such, several recent experimental implementations of significantly loophole-free tests of NC inequalities can be modified for secure RE following our approach.
2610.21765.why: Semi-device-independent randomness expansion with finite statistics from single-party N-cycle contextuality inequalities.

2610.22093.title: Bubble-Sort Exchange Networks: Symmetry Selection Rules and Language-Model Distillation on Exchange-Only Spin Chains
2610.22093.abstract: On a chain of exchange-coupled quantum dots a Heisenberg exchange pulse of area pi is a SWAP, so the parallel bubble-sort SWAP network of superconducting chains is native to exchange-only (EO) spin qubits, and any other pulse area fuses routing with an entangling interaction. We build a variational "bubble-sort exchange network" (odd-even transposition, one parameter per pulse) and study it as a Born machine read out by Pauli spin blockade. Exchange conserves total spin, so the reachable readout distributions are fixed by the total-spin content of the initial product state. For the two-spin singlet-triplet encoding we derive a selection rule -- outcomes with k triplet pairs are bounded by the initial weight in sectors S <= k (S = 0 excluded for k = 1) -- and prove by a transportation argument that it is also sufficient: the reachable distributions form the polytope cut out by the rule, and its total-variation floor is attained. Products of singlets and T0's forbid whole outcome classes; the Neel state forbids none; the three-spin EO code has no floor. We then distil, in noise-free simulation, next-token distributions of GPT-2 over restricted vocabularies into the network, with matrix-product-state (MPS) Born machines as classical control. At six logical qubits the three-spin chain reaches KL = 0.011 nat at depth N and 0.004 at 2N, below the bond-dimension-4 MPS; the two-spin chain from the Neel state reaches 0.014 at 2N and 0.004 at 3N, against 0.28-1.5 from singlet/triplet products for the first teacher. Final states lie largely outside the code space: leakage is a resource, not an error. No arrangement of disjoint pulses meets every pair in fewer than N-1 rounds, and at depth 2N the chain distils as well as a 2D array or non-local couplings. Sector-restricted simulation extends this to 10-14 logical qubits (up to 30 dots).
2610.22093.why: Exchange-only spin-chain SWAP networks obey total-spin selection rules; used to distil GPT-2 next-token distributions in simulation.

2610.19816.title: Nonadiabatic dynamics under slow parametric modulation in nonlinear graphene resonators
2610.19816.abstract: Resonantly driven nonlinear systems, from superconducting circuits to nanomechanical resonators, are often described in a rotating frame, where amplitude and phase evolve slowly within a fixed landscape of stable and unstable states. How such systems behave when this landscape moves on their intrinsic timescale remains to be understood. Here, we exploit the strong tension sensitivity of a graphene drum's resonance frequency to reshape the rotating-frame phase space of a bistable mechanical mode in real time, combining an MHz-frequency resonant drive with kHz-frequency tension modulation. When the modulation rate becomes comparable to the mechanical relaxation rate, adiabatic tracking of the fixed points breaks down. Instead, parametric instabilities emerge in the slow dynamics at frequencies set by libration around these points rather than by the mechanical resonance; stronger modulation drives period doubling and chaos. A slow-variable theory predicts where the instabilities occur, and Melnikov analysis captures the onset of chaos. These results show that the rotating frame itself can be parametrically driven, offering a general route to controlling nonadiabatic dynamics in systems ranging from Josephson bifurcation amplifiers to cold atoms.
2610.19816.why: Slow tension modulation of a graphene drum parametrically drives its rotating-frame phase space into period doubling and chaos.

2610.16286.title: Metasurface quantum graphs for polarization-independent certified randomness
2610.16286.abstract: Quantum random number generators are crucial for information security, yet existing implementations are hindered by bulky optics, device imperfections, and state alignment constraints. Here, using a compact metasurface platform, we achieve polarization-independent certified randomness by establishing a quantitative quantum graph framework. By mapping multi-channel nanophotonic responses onto graph vertices, we assign metasurface measurements an operational information-theoretic meaning, directly connecting weighted graph degrees to conditional min-entropy estimation. The resulting graph-certified measurements yield robust private randomness even under entanglement-based attacks without complex optics. Experimentally, we fabricate 4- and 6-channel dielectric metasurfaces to implement high-dimensional positive operator-valued measure graphs, successfully certifying randomness with heralded single photons and Poissonian light. By integrating complex quantum measurements into a single passive layer, our metasurface quantum graphs provide a scalable route for integrated quantum technologies.
2610.16286.why: Dielectric metasurfaces implement graph-certified POVMs for polarisation-independent randomness generation.

2610.14775.title: Driven Vortex Motion in Periodic Channel Potential Embedded in Superconducting Films
2610.14775.abstract: In this paper, we investigate vortex dynamics in periodically width-modulated superconducting channels by numerically solving the time-dependent Ginzburg-Landau (TDGL) equations. The channels are designed with sinusoidally varying widths characterized by their average width and modulation amplitude. The motion of driven vortices generates an oscillatory electric field with a fundamental frequency, $f_0$, set by the channel periodicity, together with higher-order harmonics. In contrast to the situation of vortex lattice dynamics in a periodic pinning landscape of circular holes considered by Al Luhaibi et al. [1], we show that the harmonic content of the generated electric field can be effectively controlled through the channel geometry. In particular, appropriately engineered channel profiles strongly suppress higher-order harmonics, yielding an electric-field response that closely approaches a pure sinusoidal waveform. These results demonstrate that geometric modulation offers a viable route to engineering low-harmonicity microwave signals in superconducting devices and may enable cryogenic on-chip waveform generators for controlling superconducting qubits. Such devices could provide a useful building block for scalable transmon-based quantum computing architectures.
2610.14775.why: TDGL simulations show channel-width modulation shapes the harmonic content of vortex-flow electric fields toward pure sinusoids.

2610.18418.title: The role of dependency range in thermally coupled superconducting networks
2610.18418.abstract: Interdependent networks can be highly fragile because dependency links amplify local failures into cascades that trigger global collapse. Much of the theoretical understanding comes from geometric network models, where dependency range is imposed externally and coupling strength is distance independent, and it is unclear how these insights apply to real materials, where interdependence arises from physical transport. Here we study thermally coupled amorphous superconducting networks, in which dependencies emerge from current redistribution and heat-mediated interactions governed by thermal diffusivity. Using an experimentally calibrated model of resistively shunted Josephson junctions, we show the system reproduces the three canonical transition regimes: continuous, nucleation-dominated, and mixed-order. However, because heat-driven dependency simultaneously broadens and weakens with distance, long-range thermal coupling can stabilize the superconducting phase upon heating, in contrast with its destabilizing role in geometric models. Cascades are anisotropic, with one-dimensional front propagation. These results offer an experimentally testable perspective complementing the geometric framework.
2610.18418.why: In thermally coupled superconducting networks, long-range heat coupling can stabilise superconductivity, unlike geometric interdependent-network models.

2610.15233.title: Monogamy of quantum steering in exciton--cavity optomechanical system
2610.15233.abstract: In this work, we study a theoretical scheme to investigate the monogamy of quantum steering in a hybrid exciton--cavity optomechanical (EOM) system. Within the Gaussian-state formalism, we quantify the steerability among the exciton, photon, and mechanical modes in both the steady-state and dynamical regimes. We establish and verify CKW-type monogamy inequalities for Gaussian steering and demonstrate that the distribution of bipartite steering among the three modes can be controlled through the system parameters. We further examine the influence of thermal noise and temporal evolution on the steering properties and the corresponding monogamy relations. Our results show that increasing the temperature generally suppresses the strength of Gaussian steering and modifies the degree of steering sharing imposed by the CKW-type monogamy relations. In contrast, in the dynamical regime, the steerability can increase with evolution time over suitable temporal windows, indicating that the transient dynamics can be exploited to enhance quantum correlations. These results highlight the potential of hybrid exciton--optomechanical platforms for controllable quantum correlations and provide a promising route toward the generation and manipulation of multipartite quantum resources.
2610.15233.why: CKW-type monogamy of Gaussian steering in an exciton-cavity-optomechanical model.

2610.17683.title: GWPTools: An extensible Wolfram Language framework for time-dependent Gaussian wave packet dynamics
2610.17683.abstract: Gaussian wave packets provide an exact analytical foundation for modeling time-dependent quantum phenomena, effectively bridging the gap between classical trajectories and full quantum mechanics. We introduce GWPTools, a highly extensible Wolfram Language framework designed to compute exact time-dependent Gaussian wave packet dynamics using a unified symbolic-numeric architecture. Built upon a robust ``parameter bus'' and polymorphic dispatch, the software serves as an interactive pedagogical tool for exploring quantum theory and an exact algebraic engine for rigorously benchmarking numerical grid-based and trajectory methodologies. Version 1.0.0 focuses on exact time evolution in driven one-dimensional quadratic potentials. Native extensions into quantum hydrodynamics and phase space representations enable exact energy decompositions, analytical Bohmian trajectories, and symbolic derivations of quasi-probability distributions and information metrics. We demonstrate the framework's modular scalability by prototyping interference in superpositions, open-system decoherence, and coupled two-dimensional oscillators. Ultimately, these capabilities establish a versatile foundation for maximizing the reach of exact analytical modeling toward increasingly complex driven quantum systems.
2610.17683.why: Wolfram Language package for exact Gaussian wave packet dynamics, including Bohmian trajectories, as a teaching and benchmark tool.

2610.10420.title: Lattice tuning of optical and mechanical interactions in gold nanodisk metasurfaces
2610.10420.abstract: The interaction between neighboring plasmonic nanoparticles can modify their intrinsic optical and mechanical resonances, enabling collective responses to be controlled through the geometry of their arrangement. Periodic arrays therefore provide a means of controlling both electromagnetic and mechanical interactions through a common geometrical parameter, the lattice pitch. Joint control of these two channels is particularly useful for engineering how coherent mechanical excitations couple to the substrate and are optically read out at the nanoscale. Here, we investigate the optical and mechanical response of gold nanodisk metasurface patches on silica as a function of lattice pitch using two-color pump-probe spectroscopy and numerical simulations. Optically, simulations show that varying the pitch tunes a Rayleigh anomaly across the broad localized surface plasmon resonance of the nanodisks, producing a strongly asymmetric collective optical response. Pump-probe measurements further reveal a pronounced wavelength dependence of the optical readout of coherent mechanical vibrations. Mechanically, we investigate how coupling between the nanodisks and the substrate depends on the character of the nanodisk resonances. The intrinsic nanodisk modes exhibit markedly different sensitivities to the periodic environment. One remains nearly independent of pitch, whereas another undergoes a pronounced frequency shift mediated by elastic interactions through the substrate. Numerical simulations further reveal that a third nanodisk resonance couples resonantly to a lattice-selected acoustic mode, giving rise to an avoided crossing and mode hybridization. These distinct mechanical responses are governed by how efficiently each mode couples to near-surface elastic motion in the substrate. These results demonstrate that lattice periodicity can simultaneously tune optical sensitivity and substrate-mediated mechanical coupling, providing a versatile platform for tailoring nanoscale optomechanical responses in the GHz regime.
2610.10420.why: Lattice pitch tunes optical readout and substrate-mediated acoustic coupling of gold nanodisk metasurfaces.
